hook: My brothers say I have no share in our joint family property.

slides.title: Daughters are coparceners by birth.
slides.body: In a joint Hindu family governed by Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener becomes a coparcener by birth, in her own right, in the same manner as a son.

slides.title: Same rights. Same liabilities.
slides.body: She has the same rights in the joint family (coparcenary) property as she would have had as a son, and the same liabilities.

slides.title: Father died before 2005? It still applies.
slides.body: The Supreme Court held that the father need not have been alive on 9 September 2005, when the amendment came into force. Her rights can be claimed from that date.
slides.ref: Supreme Court · Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma, 2020

slides.title: Her share equals a son's.
slides.body: When a coparcener dies on or after 9 September 2005, his share is worked out as if the property had been partitioned, and the daughter is allotted the same share as a son.

slides.title: The exception: older deals.
slides.body: Partitions, sales, gifts or wills made before 20 December 2004 are not undone. A partition must normally be by registered deed or court decree; an oral one counts only in exceptional cases backed by public documents.

slides.title: Who this covers.
slides.body: The Act applies to Hindus (including Lingayats and Arya Samaj followers), Buddhists, Jains, Sikhs, and others who are not Muslim, Christian, Parsi or Jew. It doesn't apply to Scheduled Tribes unless the Central Government notifies otherwise.

sources: Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as amended in 2005) – Sections 2, 6, 8, 10, 30
Supreme Court: Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma, (2020) 10 SCR 135
caption:
Do daughters have a share in joint family (coparcenary) property? Yes. Here's what the law says. 👇

1️⃣ A daughter becomes a coparcener by birth, just like a son
2️⃣ Same rights and same liabilities in joint family property
3️⃣ It applies even if the father died before 9 September 2005; her rights run from that date (Supreme Court, 2020)
4️⃣ Her share equals a son's share
5️⃣ Exception: partitions, sales, gifts or wills made before 20 December 2004 stand
⚠️ This is about coparcenary property. A father's self-acquired property is not a birthright. He can will it; if he dies without a will, sons and daughters inherit equal shares as Class I heirs, along with his widow and mother.

Source: Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (Sec 2, 6, 8, 10, 30); Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020)
